```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

`steCI` implements the weighted-Aalen additive-hazards sequential-trial-emulation
(STE) estimator of a causal effect on a time-to-event outcome, together with
several confidence-interval procedures. It reimplements, with citation, the
estimator of Keogh et al. (2023) and the confidence-interval comparison framework
of Limozin, Seaman and Su (2025). This manual walks through a complete analysis of
public data and documents the main arguments. The methods and their evaluation are
described in the companion paper (Karim, 2026).

## What the package estimates

From longitudinal data with a time-varying treatment and a time-varying confounder,
`steCI` emulates a sequence of trials, one starting at each visit, among subjects
untreated before the trial-baseline treatment decision. This implementation requires
absorbing observed treatment: once treated, a subject remains treated. Control-arm
rows are artificially censored when treatment is initiated, and stabilised inverse
probability of artificial-censoring weights (IPACW) correct for that censoring.
The two weight models are fitted to the control arm; treated-arm weights are one.
A weighted Aalen additive-hazards
model is fitted to the stacked trials. Two estimands are available:

* **E1, the constant hazard difference**: the coefficient of trial-baseline
  treatment in an additive-hazards model with a time-constant treatment effect.
  If the marginal effect varies over follow-up, this is a design-weighted constant
  summary that depends on the emulated-trial structure and analysis weights;
* **E2, the marginal risk-difference (MRD) curve**: always-treated minus
  never-treated risk at each horizon, obtained by standardising the fitted model
  over the empirical distribution of baseline covariates.

Because a subject who stays untreated enters several of the emulated trials, the
stacked rows are not independent. The confidence-interval functions differ in how
they handle this:

| Function | Method | Estimand | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ci_analytic()` | M1 model-based, M2 row-level robust, M3 cluster-robust SE | E1 | M3 clusters on the subject `id` |
| `ci_bootstrap()` | M4 nonparametric bootstrap of subjects | E1, E2 | refits the trials, the weights and the model in every resample; slow |
| `ci_jackknife()` | M5 delete-one-subject jackknife | E1, E2 | one refit per subject |
| `ci_lef()` | M6 linearised estimating function / multiplier bootstrap | E2 | row and cluster analytic SEs, pointwise multiplier intervals and a simultaneous (sup-*t*) band; no refitting |

The row-level robust SE (M2) treats every stacked row as independent and omits an
aggregate within-subject cross-record term; the paper recommends the subject-clustered
alternatives (M3 for E1, M6 for E2).

## Input data

The functions take **long data**: one start-stop record per subject and visit, with
columns

* `id`: subject identifier;
* `time`, `time.stop`: start and stop of the interval, in visit units (visit `k`
  starts at `time = k - 1`);
* `event`: 1 if the event occurred in the interval;
* `visit`: visit number, `1, 2, ...`;
* `A`: treatment at the start of the interval (monotone: once on, always on);
* `L`: the confounder measured at the start of the interval;
* `Alag1`: treatment at the previous visit (0 at the first visit);
* `L.baseline`: the subject's value of `L` at the first visit.

`dat_sim()` simulates data in this format (see the last section).

## Example: the Stanford heart transplant data

The Stanford heart transplant data (`survival::jasa`) record 103 patients
accepted into the transplant programme; treatment is a heart transplant, which
occurs at a time-varying point after acceptance and is absorbing, and the outcome
is death. One patient with zero follow-up is dropped, leaving 102. We use the same
preparation as the paper's application (`applied/heart_common.R` in the compendium;
the function below reproduces its `heart_to_ste()` exactly): six 30-day visits,
`A` = transplanted
by the start of the visit, `L` = standardised age, and the event = death within the
visit. Follow-up is recorded in whole days, so the times lie on a grid of 1/30 of a
visit.

```{r data}
library(steCI)

heart_long <- function(w = 30, K = 6) {
  jasa <- survival::jasa
  jasa <- jasa[jasa$futime > 0, ]            # drop zero follow-up
  Lage <- as.numeric(scale(jasa$age))        # standardised age
  rows <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(jasa)), function(i) {
    fut  <- jasa$futime[i]                   # days of follow-up
    dead <- jasa$fustat[i] == 1
    wt   <- jasa$wait.time[i]                # days to transplant (NA if none)
    k    <- 0:(K - 1)
    k    <- k[fut > k * w]                   # visits the patient reaches
    data.frame(id = i, time = k,
               time.stop = k + (pmin((k + 1) * w, fut) - k * w) / w,
               event = as.integer(dead & fut > k * w & fut <= (k + 1) * w),
               A = as.integer(!is.na(wt) & wt <= k * w),
               L = Lage[i])
  })
  d <- do.call(rbind, rows)
  d$visit <- d$time + 1
  d$Alag1 <- ave(d$A, d$id, FUN = function(a) c(0, a[-length(a)]))
  d$L.baseline <- ave(d$L, d$id, FUN = function(x) rep(x[1], length(x)))
  d
}

K <- 6       # visits (30-day months)
W <- 30      # grid points (days) per visit
d <- heart_long(w = W, K = K)
head(d)
c(rows = nrow(d), patients = length(unique(d$id)), deaths = sum(d$event))
```

### Emulating the trials

`ste_prepare()` builds one trial per visit, restricts each later trial to patients
untreated at the previous visit, censors control-arm rows when treatment is
initiated, and computes the stabilised IPACW weights
(`ipw.stab.cum`, and a version truncated at the 95th percentile,
`ipw.stab.cum.trunc`). Treated-arm weights are one under the absorbing-treatment
assumption. `time.grid = W` snaps the trial-relative times to the
exact day grid, so that deaths on the same trial-relative day are exact ties
rather than floating-point near-ties.

```{r prepare}
ds <- ste_prepare(d, n.visit = K, time.grid = W)
table(trial = ds$trial, treated_at_baseline = ds$A.baseline)
summary(ds$ipw.stab.cum)
```

### Point estimates

`ste_estimate()` prepares the trials and fits the model in one call;
`estimand = "both"` returns the constant hazard difference (`gamma`) and the
risk-difference curve (`mrd`) at the horizons `t.hor`. The heart data have many
tied death days, so we use `ties = "simultaneous"`, which enters tied events in a
single increment on a common risk set (see *Tied event times* below).

```{r estimate}
est <- ste_estimate(d, n.visit = K, t.hor = 1:K, estimand = "both",
                    ties = "simultaneous", time.grid = W)
est$gamma                                   # E1: per 30-day visit
round(setNames(est$mrd, paste0("month", 1:K)), 4)   # E2: risk difference
```

A negative risk difference means a lower risk of death under "always transplant"
than under "never transplant". No analysed death falls in the sixth trial month,
so the five- and six-month estimates coincide. The prepared data are attached to
the result as `attr(est, "dat.seq")`.

### Analytic standard errors for E1 (M1-M3)

`ci_analytic()` takes the prepared data and returns the model-based (M1),
row-level robust (M2) and cluster-robust (M3) standard errors with Wald intervals.
M3 clusters the robust variance on the subject `id`, so it accounts for a patient
contributing to several trials. Pass the same `ties` setting as the point estimate.

```{r analytic}
ci_analytic(attr(est, "dat.seq"), ties = "simultaneous")
```

The cluster-robust SE is noticeably larger than the row-level one: the row-level
SE omits the aggregate cross-record term within a patient.
(Like `timereg`, `ci_analytic()` bins clusters into at most 1000 groups; with 102
patients every patient is its own cluster.)

### Intervals and a simultaneous band for E2 (M6)

`ci_lef()` linearises the estimator through its influence functions and returns,
at each horizon, Wald intervals from the row-level and subject-clustered analytic
SEs, percentile intervals from a multiplier (wild) bootstrap of the subject-level
influence functions, and a simultaneous sup-*t* band for the whole curve. It
re-uses one fit, so the multiplier draws are cheap. It always processes tied event
times simultaneously; pass the same `time.grid`. We use `B = 200` draws to keep this
manual fast to build; the paper's application uses `B = 1000`.

```{r lef}
lf <- ci_lef(d, n.visit = K, t.hor = 1:K, B = 200, seed = 1, time.grid = W)
lf$mrd[, c("tau", "type", "estimate", "se", "lower", "upper")]
lf$band[, c("tau", "estimate", "lower", "upper")]
```

The band is asymptotically valid for the curve's fixed-weight,
fixed-standardisation linearisation under the conditions stated in the paper;
it is wider than the pointwise intervals. In the paper's simulation
its simultaneous coverage was below nominal (0.88 on average), so read it as an
approximate band.

```{r band-plot, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
pw <- lf$mrd[lf$mrd$type == "analytic_cluster", ]
bd <- lf$band
plot(bd$tau, bd$estimate, type = "s", ylim = range(bd$lower, bd$upper),
     xlab = "Month since trial baseline", ylab = "Risk difference (death)")
lines(bd$tau, bd$lower, type = "s", lty = 2)
lines(bd$tau, bd$upper, type = "s", lty = 2)
lines(pw$tau, pw$lower, type = "s", lty = 3)
lines(pw$tau, pw$upper, type = "s", lty = 3)
abline(h = 0, col = "grey")
legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", lty = c(1, 2, 3),
       legend = c("estimate", "simultaneous band", "pointwise (cluster SE)"))
```

Two optional arguments extend the multiplier bootstrap:

* `approach = "a2"` adds a first-order correction for the estimation of the
  weights (through the two logistic weight models; it requires `weight = "stab"`).
  This correction was evaluated empirically; its asymptotic validity is not
  established in the paper;
* `standardization = "random"` adds the sampling variability of the
  standardisation population, giving the unconditional variance; the default
  `"fixed"` conditions on the observed baseline covariates.

## Resampling methods (M4, M5)

The nonparametric bootstrap resamples subjects and repeats the whole analysis:
trial construction, weight models and the Aalen fit. The jackknife deletes one
subject at a time. Both are slower than the methods above (on a laptop, several
minutes for the heart bootstrap with `B = 1000` and about half a minute for the
jackknife), so they are not run when this manual is built.
Passing the full-sample estimate as `point =` centres the intervals on it; its
tie convention must match `ties`.

```{r resampling, eval = FALSE}
bo <- ci_bootstrap(d, n.visit = K, t.hor = 1:K, B = 1000, estimand = "both",
                   seed = 1, ties = "simultaneous", time.grid = W, point = est)
bo$gamma          # E1: bootstrap SE and intervals
bo$mrd            # E2: by horizon
bo$n_singular     # refits that skipped a singular risk set
jk <- ci_jackknife(d, n.visit = K, t.hor = 1:K, estimand = "both", max_n = 200,
                   ties = "simultaneous", time.grid = W, point = est)
```

The script `applied/heart_analysis.R` in the compendium runs all six methods on
these data and produces the paper's application tables.

## Tied event times

`timereg::aalen()` breaks tied event times by random jitter, so with tied data
every fit consumes random numbers and its result depends on the seed. `ste_fit()`,
`ste_estimate()`, `ci_analytic()`, `ci_bootstrap()` and `ci_jackknife()` take

* `ties = "timereg"` (the default, used in the paper's simulation study), or
* `ties = "simultaneous"`: tied events enter one increment on a common risk set,
  and no random numbers are used.

On data without tied event times the two settings agree to machine precision.
Bootstrap resamples always contain ties, because duplicated subjects share their
event times. For data recorded on a discrete sub-visit grid, set `time.grid` to the
number of grid points per visit, as above.

## Simulated data

`dat_sim()` simulates from the additive-hazard marginal structural model of
Keogh et al. (2021): an unmeasured frailty, a time-varying confounder, a monotone
treatment and a piecewise-constant additive hazard. `true_values()` computes a
Monte-Carlo approximation to the single-cohort marginal targets ("always treated"
versus "never treated" from baseline); the paper's simulation study uses the
closed-form values stored in the compendium's `dev/truth_cache_exact.rds`. The
simulated event times are continuous, so the default `ties = "timereg"` applies.

```{r simulate}
sim <- dat_sim(n = 500, seed = 1)
est_sim <- ste_estimate(sim, estimand = "both", t.hor = 1:5)
est_sim$gamma
round(est_sim$mrd, 4)
ci_analytic(attr(est_sim, "dat.seq"))
```

## References

- Karim ME (2026). Confidence intervals and simultaneous bands for additive-hazards
  sequential trial emulation. Manuscript.
- Keogh RH, Gran JM, Seaman SR, Davies G, Vansteelandt S (2023). Causal inference
  in survival analysis using longitudinal observational data: sequential trials and
  marginal structural models. *Statistics in Medicine* 42(13):2191--2225.
- Keogh RH, Seaman SR, Gran JM, Vansteelandt S (2021). Simulating longitudinal data
  from marginal structural models using the additive hazard model. *Biometrical
  Journal* 63(7):1526--1541.
- Limozin JM, Seaman SR, Su L (2025). Inference procedures in sequential trial
  emulation with survival outcomes. *Statistical Methods in Medical Research*.
